name: Khmer Empire
line: Give before you eat, walk the long way round, care for the sick and the traveller, and sit still at dusk.

quote.text: He suffered from the illnesses of his subjects more than from his own, for it is the pain of the people that is the pain of kings, and not their own pain.
quote.source: From the stele of Say Fong, about 1186, one of the foundation stones of his 102 hospitals; after the French translation of Louis Finot

quotes.text: All the beings who are plunged in the ocean of existence, may I draw them out by the virtue of this good work.
quotes.source: The king’s wish in the edict that founded his hospitals, about 1186; a common English rendering

quotes.text: These are the monuments that have led merchants from overseas to speak so often of rich and noble Cambodia.
quotes.source: A Record of Cambodia, written after his stay at Angkor in 1296 and 1297; after the translations of Paul Pelliot and Peter Harris

quotes.text: It is grander than anything left to us by Greece or Rome.
quotes.source: On Angkor Wat, from the journal of his visit in 1860, published in 1864. A French naturalist who was shown the temple by its monks

quotes.text: Negotiate a river by following its bends. Enter a country by following its customs.
Do not take the straight path or the winding path. Take the path your ancestors have taken.

words.meaning: The land of the descendants of Kambu
words.usage: The empire’s own name for itself, after a legendary hermit ancestor. Kampuchea and Cambodia come from it.
From the Sanskrit nagara, capital. The capital’s formal name was Yasodharapura, the city that bears glory.
The ending of every king’s reign name. Suryavarman is protected by the sun, Jayavarman protected by victory.
A royal cult founded in 802 that tied the kingship to Shiva. In Old Khmer it was the lord of the universe who is king.
The sanctuary tower shaped like a lotus bud. A temple may have one, five or dozens.
A rectangular lake held within earth banks. The West Baray is eight kilometres long and still holds water after a thousand years.
A dug basin with stone steps. Srah Srang, the royal bathing pool, faces the sunrise.
The lake that fed the empire. Each monsoon the river that drains it runs backwards and the lake swells to five times its size.
Hills were sacred, and where there was none the builders made one in stone.
A Buddhist monastery. Angkor Wat means the city that is a temple.

words.meaning: The mountain at the centre of the universe
words.usage: The home of the gods in Hindu and Buddhist cosmology. A temple-mountain is its image, with the moat as the surrounding ocean.
A many-headed cobra, guardian of water and ancestor of the Khmer in legend. Its body forms the balustrades of every causeway.
Spirits of the clouds and waters who dance for the gods, born from the churning of the ocean. Thousands are carved on the walls of Angkor.
The standing female figures in niches on the temple walls. Angkor Wat has nearly two thousand, no two alike.
A smooth upright stone that stood in the central shrine of a Shaivite temple and embodied the power of the god and the realm.
What gods and demons churned the ocean of milk to obtain, pulling a serpent back and forth for a thousand years.

words.meaning: The law; right order; the teaching
words.usage: The duty of a king was to uphold it. Thoa in modern Khmer.

words.meaning: The lord who looks down on the world
words.usage: The bodhisattva of compassion. The great stone faces of the Bayon are often taken to be his, with the features of the king.
The wish that others be free from suffering. Jayavarman VII made it the stated principle of his rule.
The good that comes of generous acts. To give food to monks or to build a bridge is to make merit, thvoeu bon.
A hospital. Jayavarman VII founded 102 of them across the empire, each with a chapel to the healing Buddha, staff and a fixed supply of medicines.
A stone shelter with a fire for travellers. One hundred and twenty-one stood along the raised highways, about a day’s walk apart.
Land that has been cleared, planted and brought under order, as against prey, the wild forest.
Palms together and a slight bow. The higher the hands are held, the greater the respect.
The formal greeting, said with a sampeah. Between friends it is suostei.
Arkoun chraen is thank you very much.
The classical court dance, slow and exact, descends from the temple dancers of Angkor.
Panels of pierced cowhide up to two metres tall, carried by dancers before a fire-lit screen to tell the story of Rama.
Worn by everyone as headcloth, sash, towel, sling and bag. The most Cambodian of objects.
Made each year from the huge catch of the Tonlé Sap. It seasons almost everything.

practices.name: Give before you eat
practices.instructions: Before you eat anything this morning, give something away. Put food out for someone who needs it, take breakfast to a neighbour, feed the birds, set aside money for a cause, or leave a portion of your own meal for another. Then eat. The rule of this Onda is to give first.
practices.why: In Cambodia, as across Theravada Buddhist Asia, the first food of the day is given to monks on their alms round. Giving before you eat is the lay practice that remains.
variations: Put rice in a neighbour’s bowl.
Feed the birds with breakfast crumbs.
Give a coin to a good cause before coffee.

practices.name: Walk the long way round
practices.instructions: Choose something to walk around: a building, a block, a park, a pond. Walk one complete circuit, slowly, keeping it on your right. Walk as if the wall beside you were carved and you were reading it. Look at each stretch for a moment before you move on. Pilgrims at Angkor Wat walk its galleries this way, keeping the relief on their right.
practices.why: The galleries of Angkor Wat are carved with miles of stories, read by walking round clockwise with the temple on your right. A slow circuit is a walking meditation.
variations: Notice one detail on each side.

practices.name: The sampeah
practices.instructions: Greet each person you meet today with the sampeah: press your palms together in front of you and bow your head slightly. The higher the hands, the greater the respect: at chest height for a friend, at the chin for an elder, at the nose for a monk or a teacher. Smile and say chum reap suor, hello.
practices.why: The sampeah is the Cambodian greeting, from Angkor’s carvings to today’s streets. It is graceful and respectful.

practices.name: The smile of the Bayon
practices.instructions: Stand in front of a mirror and practise the faint, serene smile of the stone faces of the Bayon, the temple of Jayavarman VII: eyes half closed, lips just curved, the whole face at rest. Hold it for a minute and breathe. Notice what it does to your mood. Wear it into the day.
practices.why: The great faces at the Bayon, with their half-smiles, are among the most famous in the world. The smile of calm compassion is something anyone can try.
variations: Smile like this at a stranger.
Do it before a hard meeting.
Look up a photo of the Bayon first.

practices.name: A bowl of rice porridge
practices.instructions: Eat bobor, rice porridge, for breakfast: simmer rice in plenty of water until soft, then add fish sauce, ginger and a little pork or fish, or keep it plain with salt and a squeeze of lime. Top with fried garlic and herbs. Eat it hot, sitting at a table. It is the everyday breakfast across Cambodia.
practices.why: Bobor is the humble comfort food of Cambodian mornings, eaten from street stalls and homes. It is warm, gentle and cheap.

practices.name: Keep the water flowing
practices.instructions: Water a plant, clear a blocked drain, mend a dripping tap or clean a bowl for birds. The Khmer built vast reservoirs, the barays, and canals to keep water flowing to the rice fields. The rule of this Onda is to keep the water flowing. Do one small thing for water today and notice where it goes.
practices.why: The kings of Angkor were hydraulic engineers, and their water network fed a million people. Caring for water is the oldest civic duty.
variations: Pour water on a thirsty tree.

practices.name: Care for the sick and the traveller
practices.instructions: Do one practical thing today for someone who is ill, or for someone who is far from home or new to the place. Bring soup or medicine. Sit with them for twenty minutes. Give directions and walk part of the way. Offer a meal. Jayavarman VII built 102 hospitals and over a hundred rest houses along the roads. The rule of this Onda is to feel others’ pain as your own.
practices.why: Jayavarman VII is remembered for building hospitals and rest houses for his people. The practice is care for those in need of help.
variations: Help a newcomer find their way.

practices.name: Train the dancer’s hands
practices.instructions: Stand with your back straight, your knees slightly bent and your shoulders down. Raise one hand to chest height and slowly press the fingers back with the other hand, as far as is comfortable, until they curve away from the palm. Hold for a breath and repeat with the other hand. Never force. Then move your arms slowly in a flowing arc. Apsara dancers train for years.
practices.why: The hands of the Khmer classical dancer curve back in a graceful arc, as seen on Angkor’s carvings of apsaras. A gentle version stretches the fingers and slows the mind.

practices.name: A game of ouk chaktrang
practices.instructions: Play ouk chaktrang, Cambodian chess, with a friend. It resembles ordinary chess, with a king, a queen who moves a single square, and a few differences in how pawns move. Learn the moves online and play a game. It is thought to have been played since the Angkor period.
practices.why: Ouk chaktrang is the Khmer cousin of chess and a source of national pride, with its own champions. It is quick to learn for any chess player.
variations: Play ordinary chess with the same spirit.

practices.name: Draw a carved scene
practices.instructions: Look at a picture of one of the bas-reliefs of Angkor Wat, such as the Churning of the Ocean of Milk, and draw a section of it. Place a sheet of thin paper over a printout and rub it lightly with a soft pencil as the visitors do, or copy by eye. Notice the rhythm of the figures. Take your time.
practices.why: The reliefs of Angkor Wat run for hundreds of metres. Drawing a few figures teaches you to see their motion.

practices.name: Build for those who come after
practices.instructions: Do one thing today that will be useful to people who come after you: plant a tree, build a bench, tidy a shared record, write down instructions for a task. Jayavarman VII built temples, hospitals and roads that lasted a thousand years. The rule of this Onda is to build for those who come after.
practices.why: The Khmer kings built for the long term, inscribing their works in stone for the future. A small act for the future is a modest echo.

practices.name: Walk by the water
practices.instructions: Walk along a river, a pond, a canal or the sea for twenty-five minutes, slowly. Look at the surface, at the birds, at the way light falls. The Khmer cities were built around water, with moats and barays reflecting the temples. Stop on a bridge and look down. Enjoy the stillness.
practices.why: Water was sacred to the Khmer, symbolising the ocean around the mountain of the gods. A walk by water has a calm of its own.
variations: Sit by the water with tea.

practices.name: Sit still at dusk with a wish for all
practices.instructions: At sunset, sit facing the fading light. Let your face soften and your eyes half close, with the faint smile of the stone faces. Breathe quietly for a few minutes. Then bring to mind one person who is suffering and wish them well: may you be free from suffering. Widen the wish to all who are ill, far from home or afraid. End with a bow.
practices.why: The Bayon’s faces are often read as faces of Lokeshvara, the bodhisattva of compassion, looking in all directions. A dusk practice of wishing well to all is in the same spirit.
variations: Name three people in your wish.

practices.name: Cook fish amok
practices.instructions: Cook amok, the Cambodian national dish: mix fish, or tofu and vegetables, with coconut milk, kroeung, a paste of lemongrass, galangal and turmeric, and an egg. Spoon it into banana-leaf cups or a bowl and steam until set like a mousse. Serve with rice. Cooking it is a gentle evening occupation.
practices.why: Fish amok is a fragrant steamed curry that is the pride of Khmer cuisine. Steaming in banana leaf gives a custard-like texture.
variations: Use tofu for a vegetarian version.

practices.name: Listen to the chapei
practices.instructions: Play a recording of the chapei, the long-necked Cambodian lute, such as Kong Nay, the blind master. Listen to the singer, who tells a story of a moral or a comic tale to a simple tune, with wit and improvisation. Sit quietly. This music is UNESCO-listed and has survived terrible times.
practices.why: Chapei dang veng is a traditional Cambodian art, a lute and a storytelling voice. Kong Nay, the blind master, was a national treasure.
variations: Look at a picture of the chapei.

practices.name: Read Zhou Daguan
practices.instructions: Read a few pages of Zhou Daguan’s A Record of Cambodia, written in 1297 by a Chinese envoy who lived at Angkor for a year. He describes the king’s processions, the markets, the women who traded and the festivals. Read it aloud and imagine the scenes. It is our best eyewitness account of Angkor.
practices.why: Zhou Daguan’s record is the only surviving description of daily life in Angkor, written by a visitor. It is vivid and full of detail.
variations: Read about the bathing of the people.

practices.name: Light a lamp
practices.instructions: Light a small lamp or candle at dusk in a safe place, as is done at Cambodian temples and in homes at festivals. Sit with it for a few minutes. Think of those who have gone before. Offer a flower beside it, if you like. Put the flame out with care when you are done. Never leave it unattended.
practices.why: Lighting lamps and candles at dusk is an ancient practice across Buddhist Asia. It marks the transition from day to night.
variations: Use a floating candle in a bowl of water.
Set a lamp by a window.

practices.name: Tell a tale from the Reamker
practices.instructions: Tell a story from the Reamker, the Khmer version of the Ramayana: the abduction of Seda, the monkey general Hanuman’s leap to Lanka or the building of the bridge. Tell it with gestures as in a shadow-puppet play. Ask the listeners who they would want to be. The Reamker is carved on the walls of Angkor.
practices.why: The Reamker is the Cambodian epic, shown in dance, masked drama and shadow puppetry. Its scenes cover the walls of the Royal Palace in Phnom Penh.

practices.name: A New Year games afternoon
practices.instructions: Play the games of Khmer New Year with friends, family and neighbours: chol chhoung, a team game in which two lines throw a twisted scarf ball to each other, boys facing girls, and the loser sings or dances; bos angkunh, tossing seeds; and tug-of-war. Splash a little water on elders’ shoulders with respect. Serve sweets and tea.
practices.why: Khmer New Year, in mid-April, is the great festival of play and family. The traditional games are great for groups.

practices.name: A day of slow circuits and water
practices.instructions: Spend a morning walking slowly round a lake, a park or a building, stopping to read each stretch as a relief. Rest by the water, sit still, share a picnic of rice and fruit with a friend. The Khmer built Angkor around water and circuits. At the end, give something away. Walk slowly and bring water and a hat.
practices.why: Walking slowly round a sacred place is a Khmer pilgrim’s practice. Doing so around a local lake or park brings its calm.
variations: End with a bowl of soup.

immersePlan.name: Read from A Record of Cambodia
immersePlan.text: Read a few pages of Zhou Daguan’s 1297 description of Angkor. Note a detail about daily life.

immersePlan.name: Read from Angkor and the Khmer Civilization
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Michael Coe’s history of the Khmer world. Note one thing about the water system.

immersePlan.name: Read from the Reamker
immersePlan.text: Read a short episode of the Khmer Ramayana in translation. Imagine it on a temple wall.

immersePlan.name: Watch Angkor: Land of the Gods
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2011 Smithsonian documentary on Angkor. Notice the aerial views of the water system.

immersePlan.name: Watch Jungle Atlantis
immersePlan.text: Watch the 2014 BBC documentary on how laser scanning revealed the huge city under the forest around Angkor.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Tenth Dancer
immersePlan.text: Watch Sally Ingleton’s 1993 film about the revival of Cambodian classical dance after the Khmer Rouge. A moving story of survival.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Homrong
immersePlan.text: Play the Royal Ballet’s overture, the traditional prelude to Cambodian classical dance. Listen to the xylophones and gongs.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Royal Court Music
immersePlan.text: Play recordings of the pinpeat ensemble of gongs, xylophones, drums and oboe. Imagine the dancers.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Kong Nay
immersePlan.text: Play the blind master of the chapei singing a comic or moral tale. Follow a translation if you can.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Churning of the Ocean of Milk
immersePlan.text: Look at the 50-metre relief at Angkor Wat of gods and demons pulling a serpent to churn the ocean. Follow the rope.

immersePlan.name: Look at the faces of the Bayon
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 216 smiling faces carved on the towers. Practise the half-smile.

immersePlan.name: Look at Banteay Srei
immersePlan.text: Look at the pink sandstone temple with exquisite carving, called the jewel of Khmer art. Notice the fine detail.

immersePlan.name: Make fish amok
immersePlan.text: Steam fish or tofu in coconut milk and kroeung paste in banana-leaf cups. Serve with rice.

immersePlan.name: Eat num banh chok
immersePlan.text: Eat fresh rice noodles with a green fish gravy of lemongrass and turmeric, topped with herbs and flowers. It is the Khmer breakfast noodle.

immersePlan.name: Make samlor korko
immersePlan.text: Make a stirring soup of vegetables, ground rice and fish, with plenty of herbs. Eat it with rice.

immersePlan.name: Drink palm juice
immersePlan.text: Drink fresh juice from the sugar palm, sold from roadside stalls in Cambodia. Use coconut water or palm sugar in water if you cannot find it.

immersePlan.name: Learn about rice wine
immersePlan.text: Rice wine is fermented from sticky rice and shared from a jar through straws at festivals. Read about it and drink a glass of cold sweet rice milk instead.

immersePlan.name: Drink sugar cane juice
immersePlan.text: Drink sugar cane juice pressed to order with a squeeze of lime and ice. Sip it slowly in the shade.

immersePlan.name: Greet with the sampeah
immersePlan.text: Greet each person today with palms together and a slight bow.

immersePlan.name: Learn temple manners
immersePlan.text: Read how visitors to Cambodian temples cover shoulders and knees, remove shoes and avoid pointing feet at Buddha images. Practise modest dress today.

immersePlan.name: Learn about the morning alms
immersePlan.text: Read about monks walking at dawn to receive food from lay people, who kneel and give in silence. Give a bowl of rice to someone who needs it.

immersePlan.name: Play ouk chaktrang
immersePlan.text: Play Cambodian chess, ouk chaktrang, or ordinary chess, with a friend, and think a few moves ahead.

immersePlan.name: Play chol chhoung
immersePlan.text: Throw a scarf ball between two lines of players, and sing a forfeit song for any miss. Play with friends.

immersePlan.name: Watch a boat race
immersePlan.text: Watch a video of the Cambodian dragon-boat racing of the Water Festival, with hundreds of paddlers. Clap along.

immersePlan.name: Mark Khmer New Year
immersePlan.text: Khmer New Year falls in mid-April. Clean the house, wash the elders’ hands with scented water and play a game.

immersePlan.name: Look up the Water Festival
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of Bon Om Touk in Phnom Penh, with boat races, lights and fireworks at the full moon of November. It marks the reversal of the Tonlé Sap’s flow.

immersePlan.name: Look up Angkor Wat
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the largest religious monument in the world. Trace the five towers at sunrise.

immersePlan.name: Practise sampeah
immersePlan.text: Sampeah is the palms-together greeting. Use it to greet three people today.

immersePlan.name: Practise karuna
immersePlan.text: Karuna is compassion. Wish well to someone who is suffering.

immersePlan.name: Think about baray
immersePlan.text: A baray is a huge reservoir built by the Khmer. Reflect on a shared resource that you rely on, and how it is kept.

rules.why: Begin the day with a gift. What you keep is not yours until you have shared.

rules.text: Feel others’ pain as your own
rules.why: Notice who is sick, poor or far from home, and act.

rules.text: Build for those who come after
rules.why: Do work that will outlast you, and do it well.
Look after what everyone depends on.
Slow, finished gestures. A calm face.
Go quietly, greet with respect and follow the custom of the place.

read.title: A Record of Cambodia: The Land and Its People
read.creator: Zhou Daguan, translated by Peter Harris
read.why: The only eyewitness account of Angkor at its height, by a Chinese envoy who stayed a year. He describes houses, clothes, bathing, markets, justice and the king’s procession.

read.title: Angkor and the Khmer Civilization
read.creator: Michael D. Coe and Damian Evans
read.why: The best single book, updated with the laser surveys that revealed the full extent of the city.

read.title: A History of Cambodia
read.creator: David Chandler
read.why: From the first kingdoms to the present, by the leading historian of the country.

read.title: Ancient Angkor
read.creator: Michael Freeman and Claude Jacques
read.why: A temple-by-temple guide with plans and photographs, by the scholar who read the inscriptions.

read.title: Reamker
read.creator: Traditional
read.why: The Glory of Rama. The Cambodian telling of the Ramayana, the story carved on the temple walls and danced ever since.

read.title: The Civilization of Angkor
read.creator: Charles Higham
read.why: An archaeologist traces the rise of the Khmer state from the rice villages of prehistory.

watch.title: Jungle Atlantis
watch.creator: BBC
watch.why: Two films on how airborne laser scanning showed the streets, ponds and suburbs of a vast city beneath the forest.

watch.title: Angkor: Land of the Gods
watch.creator: Smithsonian Channel
watch.why: The building of the empire and its temples, with reconstructions.

watch.title: The Tenth Dancer
watch.creator: Sally Ingleton
watch.why: One of the few court dancers to survive the Khmer Rouge rebuilds the Royal Ballet with her pupil.

watch.title: In the Mood for Love
watch.creator: Wong Kar-wai
watch.why: The film ends at Angkor Wat, where a man whispers a secret into a hole in the stone and seals it with mud.

listen.title: Homrong
listen.creator: Musicians of the National Dance Company of Cambodia
listen.why: Court and folk music recorded when the survivors of the 1970s had just begun to perform again.

listen.title: The Music of Cambodia: Royal Court Music
listen.creator: Recorded by David Parsons
listen.why: The pinpeat ensemble that accompanies dance, shadow theatre and temple ceremony.

listen.title: Chapei songs
listen.creator: Kong Nay
listen.why: A blind master of the long-necked lute, who sang improvised verse of wit and moral advice.

listen.title: Smot
listen.creator: Cambodian funeral chanters
listen.why: Slow, ornamented, grieving chant of Buddhist poems, sung through the night at funerals.

art.title: The Churning of the Ocean of Milk
art.creator: The carvers of Angkor Wat
art.why: Ninety-two gods and eighty-eight demons haul on the body of a serpent wound round a mountain, while Vishnu steadies it and dancers rise from the foam.

art.title: The faces of the Bayon
art.creator: The builders of Jayavarman VII
art.why: Fifty-four towers, most with four faces each, calm and smiling, in the temple at the exact centre of the capital.

art.title: Banteay Srei
art.creator: Built for the scholar Yajnavaraha
art.why: A small temple of pink sandstone carved as finely as wood, with scenes from the epics in every pediment.

art.title: Portrait of Jayavarman VII
art.creator: Unknown sculptor
art.why: A seated figure with bowed head and closed eyes, without crown or jewels. In the National Museum, Phnom Penh.

eat.title: Rice with prahok
eat.creator: Steamed rice and fermented fish
eat.why: The food of the empire’s farmers and builders, and of the countryside now.

eat.title: Fish amok
eat.creator: Fish steamed in coconut and spice paste in a banana leaf
eat.why: The national dish, perfumed with lemongrass, galangal and turmeric.

eat.title: Num banh chok
eat.creator: Fresh rice noodles with green fish gravy
eat.why: Breakfast, sold by women carrying baskets on a pole, with herbs and banana blossom.

eat.title: Samlor korko
eat.creator: A stirring soup of vegetables, fish and toasted rice
eat.why: A thick country stew that uses whatever the garden and pond provide.

drink.title: Palm juice
drink.creator: The sap of the sugar palm
drink.why: Collected at dawn by climbers on bamboo ladders. The sugar palm is the national tree.

drink.title: Rice wine
drink.creator: Fermented from sticky rice
drink.why: Zhou Daguan listed it among four kinds of wine made at Angkor, with those of honey, leaves and sugar.

drink.title: Sugar cane juice
drink.creator: Pressed to order, with a squeeze of lime

customs.title: The sampeah
customs.creator: Joined palms
customs.why: Held at the chest for equals, at the mouth for elders, at the nose for parents and teachers, at the brow for monks and the king.

customs.title: Temple manners
customs.creator: Shoulders and knees covered
customs.why: Shoes and hats come off, voices drop, and one never sits higher than a monk or points one’s feet at a Buddha.

customs.title: The morning alms
customs.creator: Rice for the monks
customs.why: Laypeople wait at their doors at dawn with food to place in the monks’ bowls, and receive a chanted blessing.

customs.title: The head and the feet
customs.creator: High and low
customs.why: The head is the most honoured part of the body and is not touched. The feet are the lowest and are kept tucked away.

games.title: Ouk chaktrang
games.creator: Board game · Cambodia
games.why: Cambodian chess, close to the ancient Indian game, with boats for rooks and fish for pawns. Players are shown at the board on the temple reliefs.

games.title: Kun lbokator
games.creator: Martial art · Cambodia
games.why: Strikes with elbows and knees, throws and weapons, with forms named after animals. Its moves appear on the walls of the Bayon.

games.title: Boat racing
games.creator: Team sport · Cambodia
games.why: Long dugout canoes with crews of sixty or more race on the river at the Water Festival, recalling the navy of Jayavarman VII.

games.title: Chol chhoung
games.creator: New Year game · Cambodia
games.why: Two lines of young men and women toss a knotted scarf back and forth and sing teasing verses.

festivals.title: Khmer New Year
festivals.creator: Three days from 13 or 14 April
festivals.why: Chaul Chnam Thmey. Houses are cleaned, elders’ hands are washed, Buddha images are bathed and everyone throws water.

festivals.title: Pchum Ben
festivals.creator: Fifteen days in September or October
festivals.why: The days of the ancestors. Families take food to the monasteries for the dead of seven generations.

festivals.title: The Water Festival
festivals.creator: The full moon of November
festivals.why: Bon Om Touk. Boat races mark the moment when the Tonlé Sap river turns and flows back to the sea.

festivals.title: Visak Bochea
festivals.creator: The full moon of May
festivals.why: The birth, awakening and death of the Buddha, kept with candlelit processions around the temples.

places.title: Angkor Wat
places.creator: Siem Reap, Cambodia
places.why: The largest religious monument in the world, built for Suryavarman II in the twelfth century: five towers inside three galleries and a moat two hundred metres wide. Go at dawn.

places.title: The Bayon and Angkor Thom
places.creator: Siem Reap, Cambodia
places.why: The walled capital of Jayavarman VII, three kilometres square, entered over causeways lined with giants pulling serpents.

places.title: Ta Prohm
places.creator: Siem Reap, Cambodia
places.why: A monastery dedicated to the king’s mother in 1186, left as it was found, with the roots of silk-cotton trees pouring over its walls.

places.title: Banteay Srei
places.creator: North of Angkor
places.why: The jewel of Khmer art, in rose-coloured stone.

places.title: Phnom Kulen
places.creator: North-east of Angkor
places.why: The sacred plateau where the empire was founded in 802. The bed of its river is carved with a thousand lingas, to bless the water flowing down to the city.

places.title: The West Baray
places.creator: West of Angkor Thom
places.why: The great reservoir of the eleventh century. People swim and picnic there, and it still irrigates the rice fields.

ethics.title: Compassion
ethics.text: Feel the suffering of others and act to relieve it.
ethics.practice: Do one thing for someone in pain.

ethics.title: Generosity
ethics.practice: Give something before your own meal.

ethics.title: Duty
ethics.text: Each person upholds the order they are part of.
ethics.practice: Do the task that falls to you, without being asked.

ethics.title: Reverence
ethics.text: Treat sacred things and elders with respect.
ethics.practice: Lower your voice and your head once today.

ethics.title: Patience
ethics.practice: Work on something you will not finish this year.

ethics.title: Humility
ethics.practice: Do something good and leave your name off it.

philosophy.title: The king’s pain
philosophy.text: Jayavarman VII declared that a ruler suffers his people’s illnesses more than his own.
philosophy.practice: Whose wellbeing are you responsible for?

philosophy.title: The mountain at the centre
philosophy.text: The temple is a model of the universe, with the capital ordered around it.
philosophy.practice: What stands at the centre of your life?

philosophy.title: Stone and wood
philosophy.text: Only gods were housed in stone. Palaces and homes were of wood and have vanished.
philosophy.practice: What are you building to last, and what to use?

philosophy.title: Water as power
philosophy.text: The realm lived by storing the monsoon and releasing it. Whoever managed the water held the kingdom.
philosophy.practice: What common resource does your community depend on?

philosophy.title: Merit
philosophy.text: Good acts bear fruit for the doer and can be dedicated to others.
philosophy.practice: For whom would you dedicate a good deed?

philosophy.title: Many gods, one realm
philosophy.text: Shiva, Vishnu and the Buddha were honoured side by side, and temples changed their dedication with the king.
philosophy.practice: What do you hold together that others think must conflict?

philosophy.title: The cost of greatness
philosophy.text: The temples were raised by the forced labour of hundreds of thousands.
philosophy.practice: Who pays for what you admire?

philosophy.title: The city the forest took
philosophy.text: A capital of nearly a million people was given back to the trees.
philosophy.practice: What that seems permanent to you is not?

journal: Whose pain did you feel as your own today?
What did you give before you ate?
What did you walk around, and what did you see?
Who was sick or far from home?
What did you do for them?
How did your hands move today?
What did the dusk bring?
Whom did you wish well?
What are you building that will outlast you?
What did you finish as carefully as carving?
What stands at the centre of your days?
What water do you depend on?
Whom did you greet with respect?
What custom of the place did you follow?
What did you do without your name on it?
Who built the things you use?
What was their labour worth?
Where did you rush?
What looked back at you calmly?
What seems permanent in your life?
What is being reclaimed by the forest?
What did an elder teach you?
For whom would you dedicate today’s good?
What did you hold together that others set apart?
What did you leave for the traveller who comes after?
Where does your responsibility end?
What did you see at sunrise or sunset?
What would you carve in stone?
What should be left in wood?
How will you begin tomorrow?
reflect: What did giving first do to your mornings?
What did you notice on your slow circuits?
What changed in the way you move?
What did the evenings of sitting give you?

intro: For six hundred years the Khmer Empire was the great power of mainland South-East Asia. From its capital at Angkor, on the plain north of the Tonlé Sap lake in what is now Cambodia, its kings ruled at their height a territory that reached into present-day Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam. They left behind more than a thousand temples, among them Angkor Wat, the largest religious building ever made. The people who built them were the ancestors of today’s Cambodians, who still call themselves Khmer.

The empire is usually dated from 802, when a prince who took the name Jayavarman II had himself consecrated on a mountain north of the lake as universal monarch, in a rite that bound the kingship to the god Shiva. His successors settled on the plain below, and around 900 King Yasovarman founded the city known as Angkor. Indian religion and learning had reached the region centuries earlier, and the Khmer court worshipped Shiva and Vishnu, wrote its inscriptions in Sanskrit and its own Old Khmer, and honoured the Buddha as well.

Angkor lived by water. The monsoon brings half a year of rain and half a year of drought, and the lake beside the city swells and shrinks with it, leaving one of the richest fisheries on Earth. Over centuries the Khmer built an immense system of canals, embankments and reservoirs, the largest of them eight kilometres long, to hold and spread the water. Laser surveys since 2007 have shown that the temples stood within a low-density city covering about a thousand square kilometres, the largest urban complex of the pre-industrial world, with perhaps three-quarters of a million people.

Each great king built a temple-mountain, a stepped pyramid crowned with towers that represented Mount Meru, the centre of the universe. In the first half of the twelfth century Suryavarman II raised Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu, its walls covered with a mile of carving. In 1177 the neighbouring Cham sacked the city. The prince who drove them out, Jayavarman VII, was a Buddhist. He rebuilt the capital as Angkor Thom around the many-faced temple of the Bayon, and covered the empire with roads, bridges, rest houses and hospitals, declaring that the suffering of his people was his own.

After him the building slowed. A gentler form of Buddhism, the Theravada, spread among the people and needed no vast temples. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries decades of drought broken by violent floods wrecked parts of the water system, while the Thai kingdom of Ayutthaya pressed from the west and trade drew power toward the coast. In 1431 a Thai army took the city and the court moved south, toward where Phnom Penh now stands. Angkor Wat was never abandoned. Monks have cared for it without a break.
The splendour had a price. The temples were built and served by forced labour and by slaves, and the inscriptions count them by the tens of thousands.

This Onda takes its practices from the reign of Jayavarman VII and from the living Buddhist culture of Cambodia: the morning gift, the walk around, care for the sick and the traveller, the dancer’s discipline and stillness at dusk.
guide.origin: Cambodia, with much of what are now Thailand, Laos and southern Vietnam
guide.era: From the consecration of Jayavarman II in 802 to the move of the court from Angkor in 1431

figures.name: Jayavarman II
figures.bio: The founder. He united rival Khmer principalities and in 802 was consecrated on Phnom Kulen as sole ruler, free of any overlord.

figures.name: Indravarman I
figures.bio: The first great builder. He dug a reservoir before he built his temples, setting the order his successors followed.

figures.name: Yasovarman I
figures.bio: He moved the capital to Angkor and built the East Baray, seven kilometres long, and a hundred hermitages.

figures.name: Kavindrarimathana
figures.bio: A Buddhist minister and the only Khmer architect known by name. He built the East Mebon and Srah Srang for a king who worshipped Shiva.

figures.name: Yajnavaraha
figures.bio: A royal grandson, scholar and physician who founded Banteay Srei. The inscriptions praise him for healing the sick and helping the poor.

figures.name: Suryavarman I
figures.bio: He won the throne after a long civil war, extended the empire westward and built the West Baray.

figures.name: Suryavarman II
figures.bio: The builder of Angkor Wat. He appears on its walls seated under fifteen parasols, and sent embassies to China.

figures.name: Jayavarman VII
figures.bio: He took the throne at about sixty after expelling the Cham and reigned for nearly forty years, building more than all his predecessors together.

figures.name: Indradevi
figures.bio: Queen of Jayavarman VII, a Buddhist scholar who taught in the monasteries and composed a Sanskrit inscription in memory of her sister, the king’s first queen.

figures.name: Jayavarman VIII
figures.bio: A devotee of Shiva under whom thousands of Buddha images were chiselled from the temple walls.

figures.name: Zhou Daguan
figures.bio: A member of a Chinese embassy who lived at Angkor for nearly a year and wrote the only surviving description of its daily life.

figures.name: Ponhea Yat
figures.bio: The last king to rule from Angkor. After its capture he founded a new capital at the meeting of the rivers.

history.detail: Trading kingdoms in the Mekong delta and then inland adopt Indian gods, writing and ideas of kingship.
Jayavarman II is consecrated on Phnom Kulen. The rite is described in an inscription written two and a half centuries later.
Indravarman I builds a reservoir, the temple of Preah Ko for his ancestors and the stepped pyramid of the Bakong.
Yasovarman I founds the city of Yasodharapura around the hill of Phnom Bakheng.
A rival king rules from a new capital a hundred kilometres away and builds a seven-tiered pyramid there.
The small pink temple is consecrated by a scholar of the court.
Suryavarman I and his successor build the largest of all the reservoirs.
Suryavarman II builds his temple and tomb in some thirty-five years, floating the stone down a canal from Phnom Kulen.
A Cham fleet sails up the river and across the lake and takes the capital by surprise.
The Buddhist king builds Angkor Thom, the Bayon, Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, with hospitals and rest houses across the realm.
Under Jayavarman VIII the state returns to Shiva and Buddhist images are defaced.
Zhou Daguan describes a rich city of gilded towers, markets run by women and a king who appears at a golden window.
Tree rings record two periods of severe drought broken by exceptional monsoons. Canals silt up and embankments are breached.
An army of Ayutthaya takes Angkor after a siege. The court withdraws to the south.

concepts.detail: The king was the protector of the realm’s sacred emblem and, after death, was united with his god. The exact meaning of the cult is still argued over.
Towers for the peaks of Meru, walls for the mountain ranges, the moat for the cosmic ocean. To build one was to put the kingdom in order.
Reservoirs, canals and raised fields evened out the monsoon. Scholars debate how much they served irrigation and how much ritual, and now agree they did both.
Shiva and Vishnu were the gods of most kings and the Buddha of some. Since the fourteenth century Cambodia has followed Theravada Buddhism.
Kings and nobles endowed temples with land, villages and workers and recorded it on stone. A temple was a religious house, a landholder and a bank.
Jayavarman VII presented hospitals, roads and rest houses as the acts of a ruler who shared his people’s pain.

concepts.text: A river that runs both ways.
concepts.detail: In the rains the Mekong forces the Tonlé Sap river backwards and the lake floods the forest. When it drains, the fish are gathered by the ton.
Free farmers owed months of work each year, and large numbers of people were bound to temples and masters as slaves.
Climate, a damaged water system, war, a change of religion and a shift of trade to the coast together drew the court away over a century.

facts.text: Angkor Wat appears on the flag of Cambodia, the only national flag to show a building of this kind.
The temple of Ta Prohm recorded that 79,365 people from 3,140 villages were needed to maintain it, including 615 dancers.
A Khmer inscription of the year 683 contains the oldest dated use of a written zero that is known.
Angkor Wat is built of between five and ten million sandstone blocks, laid without mortar.
Zhou Daguan reported that the Cambodians could harvest three or four crops of rice a year.
On the morning of the spring equinox the sun rises directly over the central tower of Angkor Wat.

sensitivity.note: The Khmer Empire is the past of a living nation, and its temples are places of worship today. This Onda was written by outsiders from published sources and draws on the public record of Jayavarman VII and on everyday Cambodian Buddhist custom. It should be reviewed by Cambodian readers.
requiredCaveats: Angkor was built by forced labour and slavery, and its kings waged constant war. The practices here take up its ideals of care, not its methods.
Cambodians lived through genocide between 1975 and 1979, in which about a quarter of the population died. Many of those who kept the arts alive were among the dead.
A great deal of Khmer sculpture was looted and sold abroad. Museums are still returning it. Buy nothing old.
If you visit, the temples are sacred. Dress modestly, do not climb or touch the carvings, and do not pose with or touch monks.
